Paid Vacation and Time-Off Policy

Purpose
This policy explains how paid vacation is accrued, requested, approved, and recorded for all regular employees of the company. The goal is to give employees predictable time to rest while ensuring business continuity during seasonal peaks, campaigns, and fulfillment deadlines. Managers and employees share responsibility for planning time away early, keeping schedules accurate, and preventing operational gaps.

Eligibility and Accrual
Full-time employees begin accruing paid vacation on their first day of employment and may use accrued time after completing 30 calendar days of service. Part-time employees who are scheduled for at least 20 hours per week accrue prorated vacation based on their standard schedule. Temporary workers, interns, and contractors do not accrue paid vacation unless a signed agreement states otherwise. Vacation is accrued each payroll cycle and displayed in the HRIS balance summary. Employees must review their balance regularly and report discrepancies to HR within five business days of noticing them.

Annual Allowance
Employees with under two years of service receive 15 vacation days per calendar year. Employees with two to five years of service receive 18 days. Employees with more than five years of service receive 22 days. Local legal entitlements that exceed this policy will always take precedence. Vacation balances may be carried over up to five unused days into the next calendar year. Any excess above the carryover cap expires on March 31 unless HR grants an exception for business-related scheduling constraints.

Request Process
Employees must submit vacation requests in the HRIS at least 10 calendar days in advance for absences of one to three days and at least 20 calendar days in advance for absences longer than three days. Requests should include dates, coverage notes, and any customer, vendor, or internal deadlines affected. The direct manager reviews the request within three business days. Approval is based on staffing levels, overlapping absences, business critical periods, and the employee's available balance. Employees should not book nonrefundable travel until approval is received in writing through the HRIS.

Blackout Periods and Coverage
The company may define limited blackout periods during high-volume events such as major promotional campaigns, year-end inventory counts, or holiday shipping peaks. During blackout periods, vacation approvals are restricted to exceptional cases, including medical needs, legally protected leave coordination, or pre-approved travel commitments documented before the blackout was announced. Each team lead must maintain a coverage plan for core responsibilities, including inbox ownership, escalation routing, and open project handoffs. Before beginning vacation, the employee must update status messages, transfer urgent tasks, and provide handoff notes to the manager or backup owner.

Changes, Cancellations, and Unplanned Extensions
If an employee needs to change or cancel approved vacation, the HRIS request must be updated immediately and the manager notified. If travel disruption, illness, or another unexpected event extends the absence, the employee should notify the manager as soon as practical and provide supporting details when requested. Approved extensions are recorded as vacation, sick leave, or unpaid leave depending on the circumstances and available balances.

Recording and Compliance
Managers are responsible for ensuring approved time-off records match actual absences. HR audits balances quarterly and may correct errors after notifying the employee and manager. Misrepresentation of time-off use, repeated failure to follow the request process, or unauthorized absence may result in corrective action. Questions about local requirements, balance calculations, or exceptions should be directed to HR Operations.
